findings.claim: Knowledge check 4: 'OCR names _____ as a separate sixth function of the skeleton, distinct from support.' options [posture, movement, balance, stability], correct = 1 (movement).
findings.truth: The answer is 'posture' (index 0). The key marked the true answer wrong; the lesson body, key fact and exam tip all teach posture as the sixth function.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1.a functions of the skeleton (support, posture, protection, movement, blood cell production, storage of minerals); lesson's own content

findings.claim: 'The hand and foot bones (carpals, metacarpals, phalanges, tarsals, metatarsals) are OCR-specific additions.'
findings.truth: The specification makes no claim about other boards, and other GCSE PE specifications name the same hand and foot bones. The comparison is removed; the bones stay on the list.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1.a location of major bones (19 named bones, matching the lesson's list)

findings.claim: Practice question 5: 'State two bones that are named in the OCR specification but were NOT required by other GCSE exam boards...'
findings.truth: The stem rests on the same unverifiable board comparison and tests nothing that is on the specification. Re-stemmed to ask for two hand or foot bones and their locations.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1.a; specification assessment section (no comparative content is examinable)

findings.claim: 'At the elbow, the humerus articulates with both the radius and the ulna - three bones meet here, which is why the elbow allows both hinge movement (flexion/extension) and some rotation.'
findings.truth: The elbow is a hinge joint. The specification allows only flexion and extension at hinge joints; forearm rotation happens at the radio-ulnar joints, not at the elbow hinge. The lesson's own key fact, knowledge check and flashcards all say flexion and extension only.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1.a types of movement at hinge joints (flexion, extension)

findings.claim: 'The roles reverse completely during elbow extension (the downward phase of a press-up): the triceps becomes the agonist...'
findings.truth: The elbow EXTENDS on the upward phase of a press-up and flexes on the way down. The phase named is the wrong one.
findings.evidence: definition of extension (increasing the joint angle) given earlier in the same unit; recomputation of the movement

findings.claim: Exam tip 'On the 8-mark Evaluate question about lever systems...' and practice question 6 typed '8 marks - Evaluate'.
findings.truth: J587/01 is a 1-hour, 60-mark paper of objective/multiple-choice, short-answer and extended-response items; the longest extended-response item is 6 marks. There is no 8-mark question and no SPaG allocation.

findings.claim: 'the effort arm (heel to Achilles insertion) is longer than the load arm (heel to ankle joint)'
findings.truth: Both arms are measured from the fulcrum, which the lesson correctly puts at the ball of the foot, not the heel. Measured from the heel the effort arm is effectively zero, since the Achilles inserts on the heel.
findings.evidence: the lesson's own second-class lever description (fulcrum = ball of the foot); definition of mechanical advantage

findings.claim: Practice question 1 keys 'a swimmer completing a 200 m race at maximum effort in approximately 2 minutes' as anaerobic, and adds 'Do not accept aerobic for full credit'.
findings.truth: A 2-minute maximal effort sits on the boundary: aerobic metabolism supplies roughly half the energy by that duration, so an absolute 1-mark key is unsafe. Two options: (a) change the stem to an unambiguous event, for example a 50 m swim in about 27 seconds; or (b) keep the stem and let the mark scheme credit either classification when it is justified by intensity AND duration. Recommendation: option (a), because a 1-mark identify question needs a single safe answer.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1.d 'apply practical examples of aerobic and anaerobic activities in relation to intensity and duration'; the lesson's own rule that a multi-minute effort at high intensity is aerobic
findings.ruling: Stem changed to a 50 m sprint (~27 s) so the 1-mark anaerobic key is unambiguous.

findings.truth: The anticipatory rise and adrenaline are not in the OCR short-term effects list and are not taught anywhere in the lesson; the check tests another board's content. Replaced with a check on muscle temperature, the first short-term effect on the specification and taught in the lesson body.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1.e short-term effects of exercise (muscle temperature; heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output; redistribution of blood flow; respiratory rate, tidal volume, minute ventilation; oxygen to the working muscles; lactic acid production)

findings.claim: 'the stork stand test (standing on one leg with the other foot resting against the knee, measuring how long balance can be maintained with eyes closed)'
findings.truth: The stork stand test is performed with the eyes open: hands on hips, the free foot against the supporting knee, the heel raised, and the time held is recorded. The eyes-closed version is the separate blind stork test.
findings.evidence: standard stork stand (Johnson and Nelson) protocol; spec 1.2.a names only the 'stork stand' test

findings.claim: 'SPOR (Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility, Recovery)... OCR uses SPOR - Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility, Recovery', repeated in the key fact, conclusion, exam tip, glossary, flashcards and knowledge checks.
findings.truth: The specification names four principles of training: specificity, overload, progression and reversibility. Overload and progression are separate principles, and recovery is not one of the four. SPOR does fit the four - Specificity, Progression, Overload, Reversibility - so the acronym is kept and the expansion corrected. The lesson's own description field already reads 'Specificity, overload, progression, reversibility'.
findings.evidence: spec 1.2.b principles of training (specificity, overload, progression, reversibility); lesson description field

findings.claim: 'it names five specific components of a warm-up and lists eight distinct physical benefits' and 'OCR lists eight specific physical benefits of a warm-up.'
findings.truth: The specification lists SEVEN physical benefits of a warm up (warming muscles/preparing the body, body temperature, heart rate, flexibility of muscles and joints, pliability of ligaments and tendons, blood flow and oxygen to muscles, speed of muscle contraction). The eight-item list is the cool-down one, which the lesson counts correctly.
findings.evidence: spec 1.2.b physical benefits of a warm up (7 bullets) vs cool down (8 bullets); the lesson's own conclusion lists the seven

findings.claim: 'keeps blood circulating so that lactic acid and carbon dioxide are transported to the liver and kidneys for processing and removal'
findings.truth: Lactic acid goes to the liver. Carbon dioxide is carried to the lungs and breathed out; the kidneys do not remove it.
findings.evidence: spec 1.1.d alveoli as the site of gas exchange; the unit's own respiratory lesson

findings.claim: 'Key sporting pairs: ... gluteals/hip flexors at the hip'
findings.truth: The pairing is anatomically right, but the hip flexors are not among the eleven muscles named in the specification, so the example cannot be credited as a named muscle. Not worth an edit.

findings.claim: The 100 m sprinter worked example lists 'muscular endurance - to sustain near-maximal effort for the full 10-12 seconds', repeated in practice question 6.
findings.truth: Muscular endurance is defined in the same lesson as repeated contractions over a long period, so applying it to a 10-second effort sits awkwardly with the definition. Defensible in some textbooks, so recorded rather than edited.
findings.evidence: spec 1.2.a definition of muscular endurance; the lesson's own definition

summary: Fourteen lessons checked against J587 Component 01. Every calculation re-derived (cardiac output, minute ventilation, mean differences) is correct. Three answer keys marked the true answer wrong or tested off-spec content (L1 posture, L5 frontal axis, L9 adrenaline), the four principles of training were wrong in L11 (recovery replaced overload/progression), and an 8-mark extended-response tariff that J587/01 does not carry appears in eight lessons.
